target_customer: Hospitals, health posts, schools, businesses and farms in Nepal and other developing countries without reliable grid power
problem: Electricity is unavailable, unstable or very expensive in much of the developing world, which blocks healthcare, education and farm productivity.
business_model: Solar installation and energy service with a US nonprofit umbrella and a for-profit entity in Nepal

founders.name: Andy Moon
founders.background_notes: HuffPost (2016-04-18). The YC page lists him as a former founder now running Reunion.

founders.name: Jason Gray
founders.background_notes: YC page says he held finance, energy and agriculture roles including general manager and vice president at SunEdison, where he set up its Canadian division. Now runs Pioneer Fund.

technical_complexity.rationale: Rooftop and off-grid solar uses commodity panels and standard installation. The difficulty was financing and logistics in remote Nepal, not engineering.

defensibility.rationale: Local presence in Nepal, nonprofit relationships such as Possible Health, and project financing know-how help, but solar installation itself is easy to copy.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent was found attempting to buy or copy the hospital solar wedge in Nepal. The YC page and website show the company still operating in Kathmandu.

market_need_then: The site states 26 percent of Nepal's population has no electricity source and 1.2 billion people lack access worldwide. HuffPost (2016-04-18) says the idea began when a doctor from Possible Health described providing healthcare without power.

branding.domain_note: Uses sunfarmer.org; the .org matches the nonprofit umbrella. Purchase history not found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Mission-led; tagline Bringing power to where it's needed the most.

branding.brand_signature: Tagline: Bringing power to where it's needed the most
branding.community_and_virality: Crowdfunded on Indiegogo with over 175 supporters per later company writing; press from HuffPost, Sustainable Brands and Globe and Mail.

brand_strength.rationale: Mission press and a crowdfunding campaign gave it some visibility, but no evidence the name or visual brand drove customers.

outcome_analysis: SunFarmer was started in 2012 by two former SunEdison employees to power Nepali health clinics, funded early by a SunEdison foundation grant and an Indiegogo campaign, then joined YC in 2015. It is still operating in Kathmandu and reports pumped water and clean electricity totals. Both founders have since moved to other ventures. The business is mission-driven and venture funding found is small, so its trajectory is stable but modest.
notes: Unverified aggregator figures: 120K dollars YC round dated March or April 2016 (Persana, CB Insights) while HuffPost and a founder post disagree on YC Summer vs Winter; a 25K dollar Indiegogo goal in 2014 was reported reached by a later article but not recorded as a round. The 2M dollar SunEdison figure is a project grant per one report, another says partial funding by SunEdison Rural Energy Fund. Competitors: no source dated near 2015 compares rivals, and 2024 listings of d.light, Azuri and Off-Grid Electric are excluded.
